notes.meaning: After the sin of the golden calf, God and Israel have made peace again. Now the work of setting up God's worship starts once more. Moses gathers the people and passes on only what God told him, nothing added or left out. Matthew Henry thinks the whole congregation here means the leaders of each tribe, who would then tell everyone else.

Before any building begins, God's people are reminded to rest. They could work on the tabernacle (God's tent for worship) for six days, but not on the seventh. The holy day ranked even above the holy place. The death penalty shows how serious the Sabbath was as the sign of God's covenant, His binding promise, with Israel. Henry also sees this rest as a picture of the lasting rest waiting for God's people (Hebrews 4:9).

No fire was to be lit on the Sabbath. Wesley and Henry say this meant fire for work, like a metalworker's fire. Keil and Delitzsch note the rule held even for the tabernacle work. Gill thought it may have been a short-term rule tied to the building, since care for the sick or babies would still need fire.

Moses now starts carrying out what God told him in Exodus 25–31. Much of this chapter repeats those earlier chapters. The repeating is on purpose. It shows Moses was faithful in doing just what God said.

The gift was for the Lord Himself, because the tabernacle was His. It was not a tax. Only those with a willing heart were to give, because God loves a cheerful giver. God could have supplied everything by a miracle. Instead He let His people share in the work by giving freely.

These are the same materials listed back in Exodus 25. Calvin asks how a poor people, so lately slaves, could own such riches. His answer is that God gave them the wealth of Egypt when they left. Now they could give it back to Him gladly.
The list goes on with oil for the lamps and spices for the holy oil and incense. It also names precious stones for the high priest's special clothes. Each item had been described in detail earlier.

Next Moses calls on the skilled workers, people the Bible calls "wise-hearted." God gives different gifts to different people. The rich brought materials and the skilled brought their skill. Each needed the other, and the work needed both (1 Peter 4:10).

Moses gives a short list of everything to be made, starting with the tent and the ark. Calvin says the summary was meant to stir them up, since teaching is often received coldly without some encouragement. The veil hung in front of the mercy seat so it could not be seen. Henry says the list showed how much work lay ahead, so every hand would get busy.

The list goes on with the lampstand, the golden altar for incense and the bronze altar for burnt offerings. It also includes the washing basin. All of these had been described before in Exodus 25, 27 and 30.

The list ends with the courtyard curtains, the tent pegs and their ropes, and the clothes for the priests. Even small things like pegs and ropes are named. Clarke thinks the "woven garments" may have been everyday cloths, like aprons and towels. These were different from the holy clothes for Aaron and his sons.

The people went home to their tents. There were no exciting speeches, and no one was pushed to make a public promise. They trusted that Moses had told them God's will. Henry stresses that they acted quickly. Calvin adds that they thought it over in private, which makes their giving even more worthy of praise.

Their hearts were "lifted up" to give. No one forced them. They gave out of love for God, thanks for what He had done, and faith in His promises. Calvin adds that God's Spirit was at work inside them, moving them to want to give. The gifts went to the Lord, not to Moses.

Men and women brought their gold jewelry, and the wording suggests the women came first. In those days there were no coins, so jewelry was a kind of money. Giving it up showed real love for God. Henry thinks the memory of the golden calf may have made them eager to give now, as a sign they were sorry. A "wave offering" was a gift dedicated to the Lord, once marked by moving it to and fro.

Each person brought what they had. Those without gold brought goat hair, skins, silver, bronze or wood. God looks more at the heart of the giver than at the price of the gift (2 Corinthians 8:12). Calvin says the poor could be sure their small gift pleased God as much as a rich person's large one.

Skilled women spun yarn by hand. Some spun fine colored thread and others plain goat hair, yet both are called wise. God accepts humble work as well as fine work. Someone faithful in a lowly job is as accepted by God as someone in a grand one. The goat hair was for the outer covering of the tent.

The leaders brought the costly things, like precious stones, spices and oil. They were wealthier and could give the rarer items. Ellicott suggests these were the twelve tribal leaders. Each may have given the stone that bore his own tribe's name. Clarke loves how everyone joined in, from rulers to women spinning.

It was all a freewill offering, a gift given by choice. No one was forced. Clarke says this was the first way God's people paid for a place of worship. He calls it a privilege to give anything for God's house.

God Himself chose Bezalel by name to lead the work. This kept people from arguing over who was in charge, because God is a God of order. It also assured the people that the men handling their gold were picked by God. Calvin says it encouraged them to see that God was over the work.

God filled Bezalel with His Spirit and gave him great skill. Calvin says these gifts were not simply natural or earned. Henry adds that skill even in ordinary work is a gift from above (James 1:17) and should be used for God's honor. Because the work was special, God gave him special help, much as He later filled the apostles for building the church.

Bezalel could design and work in metal, stone and wood. These verses repeat Exodus 31 almost word for word. Henry notes he was to do the work himself, not just plan it. People with great gifts must not use them as an excuse to sit idle.

God also gave Bezalel and Oholiab the ability to teach. They trained and guided the other workers. Calvin says two men could never have finished alone, so teaching was a gift too. Henry says leaders should teach, and those who know much should share it.

God filled these men with skill for every kind of craft, from engraving and design to weaving and embroidery. This shows that skill in art is a gift from God. Calvin explains that "wisdom of heart" means ability of the mind, not just feelings.
